info.title: keyext.server
info.description:
A headless JSON-RPC interface to the KeY theorem prover, for automated agents.

One rule governs everything here: the only legitimate source of 'this is verified' is KeY's own Proof.closed(), reported as Statistics.closed. No error path, no timeout, no task reaching SUCCEEDED may be read as a closed proof. A task that finished is a task that finished.

Transport: POST /rpc for calls, GET /rpc for a Server-Sent Events stream carrying task.progress and task.finished as JSON-RPC notifications. Bound to 127.0.0.1 only; there is no authentication, so reach a remote instance through an SSH tunnel.

Third-party tool, not an official KeY component.

methods.name: proof.save
methods.summary: Write a proof to disk in KeY's own format.
methods.description: Until a proof is written out it lives only as long as this server, which makes every result unreviewable: there is nothing to read, re-check or commit. The format is KeY's, so the file can be loaded by KeY itself and not only by this server.

params.description: Relative paths are taken against the workspace. When omitted the proof is named after itself, in the workspace.

params.description: Write a .zproof bundle carrying the sources, not a bare .proof.

methods.name: diagnostics.listApplicableRules
methods.summary: List the rules that could still be applied to a goal by hand.
methods.description: Refused while a task is working on the proof, for two reasons: the probe builds rule applications against live goal state, and KeY consults its interactive rule index only while no automatic search is running — asked during one it would quietly answer from the strategy-filtered subset instead.

EnvironmentRef.description: Opaque handle on a loaded project. Pass it back as received; never build one.

GoalRef.description: Opaque handle on one goal of one proof. KeY numbers nodes per proof, so a goal has no identity outside its proof and the reference carries both halves.

Ok.description: The request was carried out. Never a statement about a proof.

SourcePosition.description: A place in a source file KeY attached to a failure.

ErrorData.description: Machine-readable detail on an error. Branch on the numeric code, never on message text.

TaskStatus.description: SUCCEEDED means the work finished without throwing. It does NOT mean a proof closed. A macro that runs to its end leaving three goals open is a SUCCEEDED task with three open goals; only Statistics.closed answers the other question.

TaskHandle.description: The state of one long-running operation.

subject.description: What the task operates on: an EnvironmentRef or a ProofRef.

result.description: The product of a succeeded task.

ProofObligationKind.description: INFORMATION_FLOW is only produced when a provider of KeY's InformationFlowContractSupplier is on the class path, which this build does not ship. OTHER is reported rather than guessing at a kind that might be wrong.

contractId.description: KeY's unique internal contract name. Pass it to proof.start.

targetMember.description: Signature such as add(int, int); the parameter types distinguish overloads.

Statistics.description: What is known about a proof. `closed` is the only field that answers whether anything was verified, and it is read from KeY's own Proof.closed() every time this object is built: never cached, never defaulted, never inferred from a task having finished.

AutoModeOutcome.description: Why the search stopped. None of these says anything about success. What they do say is whether more of the same would help: MAX_RULES, BUDGET_ELAPSED and STRATEGY_TIMEOUT mean the search was still working when it was stopped, while EXHAUSTED means the prover did everything it knows and the goals left need a script, a solver or a specification rather than more time.

AutoModeResult.description: The result member of a finished AUTO task.

ProofRunResult.description: The result member of a finished MACRO or SCRIPT task.

GoalSummary.description: goalId and nodeId are the same number today: KeY identifies a goal by the serial of the node it sits on. Both are reported because they are used in different places and a client should not have to know they coincide.

SequentFormat.description: TEXT is KeY's pretty-printed rendering, UNICODE the same with logical symbols, and STRUCTURED the same again with each formula also taken apart into its symbolic state, the program still to run, and what must hold once it has.

formulas.description: Present only for STRUCTURED. antecedent and succedent are present regardless.

macroId.description: Also the macro's name inside a proof script.

StuckReason.description: NEEDS_SPEC is asked of KeY's own rule application - whether a loop invariant application found an invariant, whether a contract application found a contract - not inferred from the rule's type. Where that cannot be established the answer is NOT_INSTANTIABLE rather than a cause that might be wrong.

StuckPoint.description: A rule that KeY would like to apply to a goal and cannot.

ruleId.description: Stable identifier: the rule's implementation class name.

source.description: Where in the Java source this points, when it points anywhere.

GoalDiagnostics.description: An empty stuckPoints list is a finding, not a blank: no built-in rule applies here, so the goal is not waiting on a missing specification. Read it with lastSearchOutcome to tell a prover that ran out of ideas from one that ran out of budget.

truncated.description: The probe reached its depth ceiling before the end of a formula.

lastSearchOutcome.description: How the last automatic search on this proof ended, absent when none has run. Read an empty stuckPoints list together with this: empty after EXHAUSTED means the prover tried and ran out of ideas, empty after a limit means it never finished looking. The two are the same list and opposite problems.

SavedProof.description: Where a proof was written. That this object exists at all means the file is on disk: a save that did not happen is reported as an error, never as a path.

EnvironmentLoaded.description: What a finished LOAD or REPLAY task produced. A .proof or .zproof file brings a proof with it; the field is absent for a project or a problem file that declares none.

SequentSide.description: Which side of the turnstile a formula sits on: assumed, or to be shown.

StructuredFormula.description: One formula taken apart. A proof obligation in mid-flight prints as a single formula several hundred characters long whose interesting part is the last thirty; separated, each piece answers a different question and can be read on its own. The split is KeY's own, taken from the position table it builds while printing, so it cannot drift from what KeY thinks the formula is.

index.description: Position within that side, matching the antecedent or succedent array.

state.description: The symbolic state (KeY's update). Absent when there is none.

program.description: The Java still to be executed. Absent when there is none.

claim.description: The formula with the state and the program elided, marked with an ellipsis: what remains to be shown about them. For a formula with neither, the whole formula.

RuleKind.description: How a taclet finds what it applies to. KeY's categorisation, not an assessment.

ApplicableRule.description: A rule that applies to a goal here and now, with one entry per place it applies. A rule listed several times matches several times, which is what makes a script's bare `rule "name";` refuse it as ambiguous.

ruleId.description: The taclet's name, which is what a proof script's rule command takes.

index.description: The formula on that side. Absent for NO_FIND.

needsInstantiation.description: Schema variables remain to be filled in, with inst_… in a script.

needsAssumption.description: The rule has an \assumes clause and no instantiation has been chosen.

GoalRules.description: What could still be applied to a goal by hand: the complement of stuck points. Those say what wants to apply and cannot; this says what could apply and the automatic strategy did not choose, which after a search that came back EXHAUSTED is what is left to look at. No judgement is offered about which are worth trying — cut and hide_left apply almost anywhere — and nothing is promised about applying one straight away: the obstacles reported are those visible from a survey of the top level of each formula, so a rule listed once may still match inside a term. Candidates, not promises.
